voice: ElevenLabs Lily, directed per line kind
note: Hand-written script, spoken verbatim, and the pictures written to match it. Each screen carries what she says, what the picture must show, and the points she can be asked about; the locator only finds where each named point sits. A fact appears exactly once in the whole tour.

arrival.line: Hello, and good morning. My name's Nell Baker, and I sell flowers here at the top of Ludgate Hill, violets mostly, and watercress when the season's right. I've been doing it for nine years now, so I know this street better than I know my own front door. What I'd like to do is walk you all the way down it, from here to the river, and tell you about the place as we go. There are six stops along the way, and we'll take them slowly. If you see something you're curious about, just touch it and I'll tell you what it is, and if you'd rather simply ask me, hold the green button and talk, and I'll answer you as best I can. So, here we are. It's the spring of 1850, and this is Ludgate Hill.
arrival.scene: Ludgate Hill, London, spring 1850, from the pavement halfway up, looking east. The west front and dome of St Paul's Cathedral close the top of the street with clear sky behind it and nothing built across the view. A green horse-drawn omnibus crammed with passengers, several seated on the roof, climbs at walking pace in the middle of the road. Near the front on the right, a boy of about twelve in ragged clothes sweeps a crossing clear with a long broom. Shopfronts with painted signboards on both sides, top hats and shawls, wet granite setts.

points.label: St Paul's
points.line: That's St Paul's up there, and that's where we're headed. It's the tallest thing in London by a long way, so if you ever find yourself turned around on this side of the river, just look up and you'll know where you are.

points.label: green omnibus
points.line: You could ride that if you had sixpence to spare, but I never do. My money is stock money and it all goes on flowers, so I walk instead and put the difference towards tomorrow's market.

points.label: crossing boy
points.line: That boy there is the reason your boots are still worth looking at. There's no drain in this road, so everything the horses leave behind just sits where it falls, and he sweeps a clean path across it for anyone who wants to cross. He'll be at that until the light goes.

stop_01_ludgate_hill_c1.narration: By seven in the morning this hill is as busy as it ever gets, and I have to say I love it. Every cart and cab and omnibus you can see is carrying something that has to be sold before dark, and everyone driving them knows it. I come up through the middle of all this twice a day with my basket on my hip, and you do learn to step lively, because nobody here waits for anybody.
stop_01_ludgate_hill_c1.scene: The roadway of Ludgate Hill at seven in the morning, 1850, close in at eye level. A green horse-drawn omnibus fills the middle with passengers packed along the knifeboard seat on its roof in the wind. Beside it a brewer's dray heaped with chained wooden barrels, drawn by heavy horses. The soot-blackened upper stonework of St Paul's rises behind, dark on its weather side. Carts, cabs and walking traders crowd every gap.

points.label: St Paul's dome
points.line: Look how black the stone has gone on that side of the church. That's coal smoke. Every house in London burns coal, all day and all winter, and the church just quietly wears the soot like an old coat.

points.label: the omnibus
points.line: That's how the clerks get to work in the morning, and you can always tell the ones who couldn't afford to be late, because they're sitting up on the roof in the wind rather than paying for a seat inside.

points.label: the dray barrels
points.line: Those are brewers' drays, and they go at their own pace and ask nobody's permission. Everything on this hill is either pulling a load or getting out of the way of something that is.

stop_01_ludgate_hill_c2.narration: Stop for a moment and look at what the whole street is pointing towards. You see how the roofs step down on either side, lower and lower as they go? That leaves the church standing there with the sky all to itself. There's nothing built across it and nothing built over it, not so much as a railway bridge. People walk up this hill every day of their lives and never once look up. I still do.
stop_01_ludgate_hill_c2.scene: Ludgate Hill, 1850, looking straight up the street to St Paul's Cathedral, which stands with the whole sky to itself, nothing built across or over it. The roofs of the shops step down on both sides towards the viewer. On the left near the front, a coffee house with a painted signboard over its door. A horse-drawn omnibus takes the centre of the road at walking pace. Overcast light, coal haze.

points.label: St Paul's dome
points.line: A man named Christopher Wren built that church, and it took him the best part of his life. It was finished in 1711, which means people were born, learned a trade and were buried again while it was still going up.

points.label: coffee house sign
points.line: That's a coffee house, and there'll be a stall out on the pavement beside it before five in the morning. A good many trades round here start work long before there's any light to see by.

points.label: omnibus
points.line: Watch how it takes the middle of the road and dares anyone to argue. The hill is steep enough that the horses have to walk it, which means everything behind them walks it too.

stop_01_ludgate_hill.transitionOut: Come along with me now, up past the booksellers' windows. I want to show you what stands at the top of this hill, and what's grown up right against its walls.

arrival.line: Here we are, and this is my corner. Now, you might expect a cathedral to have a bit of quiet green around it, but this one doesn't get anything of the sort. The shops come right up to the railings, drapers and booksellers and milliners and chemists, all of them pressed in as close as they're allowed. I stand just here because this is where the crowd is thickest, and a crowd is really the whole of my living.
arrival.scene: St Paul's Churchyard, London 1850, from the pavement. The cathedral's dome and upper front rise beyond iron railings on the right, dulled by soot. Shops crowd right up to the railings on the left, one of them a tea merchant with a large painted signboard. In the near foreground a woman's wicker flower basket brimming with violet bunches rests on a low step. Clerks and shoppers pass close by.

points.label: St Paul's dome
points.line: The clock inside there empties straight into the street. When the service ends the doors open and my corner is suddenly worth standing on, and once everyone has gone I might as well be selling to the pigeons.

points.label: Tea merchant sign
points.line: That's a tea merchant, and behind that window there'll be a counting house full of clerks. They come out at noon with a few coppers in their pockets and no clear idea what to do with them, which suits me very well.

points.label: Flower basket
points.line: That's my stock there, and all of it has to be sold today. Flowers keep about as well as fish, so what smells sweet this morning is rubbish by tomorrow, and there's no putting any of it aside.

stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard_c1.narration: I'm over at Farringdon market by four in the morning to buy, while most of the city is still asleep. A shilling gets me a dozen bunches wholesale, and I sell them on at a penny each, provided they keep their sweetness and provided it doesn't rain. Some days that comes home nicely. Other days I carry the lot back again in the evening, and then it's just dead weight.
stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard_c1.scene: A flower seller's pitch at the corner of St Paul's Churchyard, 1850. The cathedral front stands behind, sooty above and hemmed below by shopfronts. In the near foreground her wicker basket of violet bunches sits at hand height. On the left, a grocer's shopfront with its painted signboard and window of goods. Clerks in dark coats pass at midday.

points.label: St Paul's front
points.line: On a bad morning you can lose the whole of that dome in the smoke by about ten o'clock, cross and all, standing exactly where I'm standing. It comes back by noon if the wind is kind to us.

points.label: violet basket
points.line: Violets sell to gentlemen on their way in to dine, and to young men who've done something they're sorry for. I can spot the second sort from twenty paces, and I always let them pay first.

points.label: grocer's sign
points.line: The shops will buy my watercress straight off me if it looks big and fresh, and a shopkeeper pays a good deal quicker than a crowd does. Cress is a breakfast, mind, so it has to be gone by eight or not at all.

stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard_c2.narration: Look at the way the shop fronts press up against the church, sign above sign above sign. For two hundred years this yard was where England came to buy its books, and the trade never really left. It only moved a street back and carried on quietly. There's more paper bought and sold within a hundred paces of where we're standing than anywhere else in the country.
stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard_c2.scene: St Paul's Churchyard, 1850, the row of shops packed hard against the cathedral, sign above sign. The dome shows above the roofline through smoke. On the left a bookseller's hanging sign over a window of stacked books. In the middle distance a boy hurries along the pavement with a large brown paper parcel under both arms.

points.label: St Paul's dome
points.line: Booksellers along there, and printers behind them, and behind those the men who carry it all. If you buy a book anywhere in the country, the chances are it was made within a quarter mile of this railing.

points.label: bookseller sign
points.line: That lad is carrying somebody's whole day in his arms. Boys like him are the post of this quarter, because they go faster than a cart through these streets and they cost a great deal less than a horse.

stop_02_st_pauls_churchyard.transitionOut: Now come round the back of the church with me, into what I think is the narrowest street in the whole city. You'll smell the paper before you see it.

arrival.line: This is Paternoster Row, and it's barely a street at all. In places two carts will fill the whole width of it, and the houses stand up so tall on either side that you almost have to send for the daylight. Behind every one of those windows somebody is printing, or binding, or selling what's been printed. This little lane is where the words come from.
arrival.scene: Paternoster Row, London 1850: a very narrow street with tall sombre houses on both sides leaning over it, daylight only in a strip above. The dome of St Paul's shows beyond the roofs at the end. Bookseller and publisher signboards hang from the buildings on the left. In the middle of the lane a man pushes a handcart stacked with brown paper parcels.

points.label: St Paul's dome
points.line: The church is right behind those roofs, not a hundred paces away. This row has always lived in its shadow, and that's how it got its name, from the prayer that people said as they walked around the cathedral.

points.label: bookseller's sign
points.line: Every sign along here says the same thing under a different name. When one trade takes over a street entirely the rents follow it up, and after that no baker or butcher can afford to stand among them.

points.label: parcel handcart
points.line: Handcarts rather than wagons, you'll notice. A wagon simply can't turn in this row, so the paper goes out by hand as far as the wider streets, and only then does it get loaded properly.

stop_03_paternoster_row_c1.narration: There's hardly room here for any other trade at all. The booksellers and publishers took this row a long time ago and they've kept it ever since. What you're seeing on the pavement isn't customers, it's porters, and they're carrying parcels out to every town in England, and carrying them back again when they don't sell.
stop_03_paternoster_row_c1.scene: Inside Paternoster Row, 1850, hemmed in: pinched pavement, tall dark house fronts, and a publisher's painted signboard prominent on the left. Two porters in aprons carry heavy corded parcels of books at a trot along the narrow way. On the right, the mouth of a covered court cuts through the buildings as a dark archway.

points.label: bookseller sign
points.line: That's a publisher's board. The man whose name is on it never touches the paper himself. He pays the printer and he pays the binder, and he carries the risk of the whole edition on his own head.

points.label: parcel porters
points.line: Those men are carrying loads that would put me on my knees, and they do it at a trot all day. Ask any one of them what's in the parcel and he'll tell you quite cheerfully that he's never opened one in his life.

points.label: court arch
points.line: Through that archway there's a little court, and through the court you come out in the churchyard. The whole quarter is stitched together with holes in the wall like that one, and a stranger would never find them.

stop_03_paternoster_row_c2.narration: Keep yourself against the wall when a cart comes through, because there's nowhere else to go. Those little courts running off the row aren't there for prettiness either. They're the way out when the street gets blocked, and every porter round here knows them better than he knows the row itself.
stop_03_paternoster_row_c2.scene: The narrowest part of Paternoster Row, 1850, with two carts almost filling the width of the street between the tall houses. In the middle of the row, a stone archway opening into a small court, its name painted above. Bookshop windows and hanging trade signs along both sides.

points.label: the court archway
points.line: That's Lovell's Court. Courts like it usually hide a printing house or two, tucked away out of sight, and the sound of the presses comes up out of them like something breathing.

points.label: two carriages
points.line: Two of them, and the street is completely full. When a cart stops here to unload, everything behind it stops as well, and a great deal gets said about it while they wait.

stop_03_paternoster_row_c4.narration: Now this is the whole business, really, in one picture. One man reads and everybody else leans in to listen. There's a new weekly out this spring called Household Words, and it costs twopence, and twopence will do for a dozen listeners as long as one of them has his letters. That's how the news reaches people like me, out loud, and second hand.
stop_03_paternoster_row_c4.scene: A knot of working people gathered on the pavement of Paternoster Row, 1850. In the centre a man in a cap holds an open twopenny weekly and reads aloud; the others lean in to listen, some in aprons, one with a basket. A bookseller's painted signboard hangs above them on the left.

points.label: the reader
points.line: He isn't showing off, by the way. Plenty of the people standing there can't read a line for themselves and would far rather hear it read aloud than own the paper, so a man with a clear voice is never short of company.

points.label: bookseller sign
points.line: Twopence for one of those, mind, when a loaf of bread costs more than fivepence. Reading has become cheap in a way it simply never was before, and that's a much newer thing than you might imagine.

stop_03_paternoster_row.transitionOut: Right, that's enough print for one morning. We're going west from here, where the road widens out and the traffic doubles, so stay close to me. I want to show you something that isn't there at all.

arrival.line: This is Fleet Street, and that arch you can see ahead of us is Temple Bar, the old gate of the city. Anything coming in or going out this way has to squeeze underneath it, which is why nothing here ever moves faster than a walk. And there's a river under your feet, though you'd never know it. The Fleet runs beneath this road, covered over the whole way down to the Thames.
arrival.scene: Fleet Street, London 1850, looking towards Temple Bar, the smoke-blackened stone gateway arch spanning the road ahead with traffic funnelling under it. On the right a small coffee stall on the pavement with a steaming urn and men standing at it. In the near left foreground, iron gratings set into the kerbside gutter of the roadway. Cabs, carts and an omnibus press towards the arch.

points.label: Temple Bar
points.line: Christopher Wren built that one too, after the Great Fire, and it's been narrowing this road ever since. There's talk of pulling it down to let the traffic through, and there's been talk of that my whole life.

points.label: coffee stall
points.line: Stalls like that will stand there all night. The printers work while the town sleeps, and printers have to eat, so there's always something hot to be had on Fleet Street at three in the morning.

points.label: road gratings
points.line: Put your ear near one of those gratings after a heavy rain and you'll hear it. There's a whole river down there in the dark, running along under the shops as though nothing had ever happened to it.

stop_04_fleet_street_c1.narration: A coffee stall does its best trade at either end of the day, in the dark before work starts and the dark after it finishes. It's a penny for a mug and a halfpenny for a half. For a good many of the people standing at that stall, that is breakfast, and there'll be nothing else until night.
stop_04_fleet_street_c1.scene: A Fleet Street coffee stall at first light, 1850, close in: a trestle stall with a large tin urn, mugs, and a plate of thin bread and butter, the stallholder serving working men and clerks. Temple Bar's arch stands further along the street behind them. Above on the right, a coffee house signboard with booksellers' windows below it.

points.label: coffee stall
points.line: Bread and butter at the stall, cut thin, with a bit of my watercress laid over it if I've any left by then. That's what a working breakfast looks like, eaten standing up.

points.label: Temple Bar
points.line: Underneath that arch is the boundary. On this side the city keeps its own constables and its own rules, and one step through and you're in Westminster's world, where the law changes along with the paving.

points.label: the coffee house sign
points.line: That's a coffee house where the newspapers are taken, and anyone who buys a cup may read them. That's Fleet Street entirely, really. Print upstairs, news downstairs, and something hot in between.

stop_04_fleet_street_c2.narration: The Bar isn't there for show. It marks where the city begins, and even the Queen has to stop at it and ask leave before she comes through. The rest of us don't ask, of course. We just wait our turn, which somehow takes rather longer.
stop_04_fleet_street_c2.scene: Temple Bar, London 1850, seen from Fleet Street: the sooty stone archway across the road, an omnibus with passengers on the roof passing beneath it with barely an inch to spare, and a hackney cab close on the right waiting its turn. Crowds on foot squeeze along the edges.

points.label: the omnibus
points.line: The omnibus has to go under with about an inch to spare, and the men riding on the roof duck without being told. Every one of them has done it a hundred times before.

points.label: the cab
points.line: A cab is for people whose time is worth more than their money, and there are more of them on this street than any other I know, because a newspaper man is always late for something.

stop_04_fleet_street_c4.narration: Last year the cholera came through London, and in the city alone they buried three thousand seven hundred and sixty three people. The doctors told us it was the bad air that carried it, so we all learned to be afraid of a smell. The Fleet is running under that grating there, and everything this street pours away goes down with it.
stop_04_fleet_street_c4.scene: A flower seller's basket of violets held above an iron gutter grating in the Fleet Street roadway, 1850, close in at waist height. Further left along the pavement stands a coffee stall with its urn. Temple Bar's dark arch closes the street in the distance. Damp, smoky air.

points.label: violet basket
points.line: My flowers do a kindness here that has nothing to do with selling. A bunch of violets held up under the nose is what a lady does when she has to walk past a grating in July.

points.label: Temple Bar
points.line: Beyond the Bar the road carries on to Westminster and the Parliament house. Whatever we tip into the Fleet ends up in the river, and the river runs right past their windows too. They'll find that out eventually.

stop_04_fleet_street.transitionOut: Now let's walk down towards the water together. Where the Fleet comes out into the Thames there's a bridge, and from the middle of it you can see what this city actually runs on.

arrival.line: This is Blackfriars Bridge. Stand at the parapet with me for a minute and look both ways at once, because there are carts on the stone above us and boats on the water below, and the gas works across the way making the smoke that hangs over the lot of it. The Thames isn't scenery, whatever anyone tells you. It's the busiest road in England, and it never closes.
arrival.scene: On Blackfriars Bridge, London 1850, at the stone parapet. Below on the river a paddle steamer with a tall funnel drives through the water trailing smoke. Along the bridge roadway, carts, cabs and driven animals cross in both directions. Across the water, the chimneys of a riverside gas works pour dark smoke into the sky.

points.label: river steamer
points.line: The penny steamers run to a timetable, which is quite a new thing on this river. A waterman went when he had a fare and not before, but the steamer goes whether you're aboard or not.

points.label: bridge traffic
points.line: Everything crosses here. Droves of animals on their way to market, brewers' carts, cabs, and people on foot keeping well to the sides. This bridge earns its keep from before dawn until long after dark.

points.label: gas-works smoke
points.line: That's the gas works over there, and that smoke is what lights the shop windows and the street lamps you'll walk home by. They build them on the riverbank because the coal comes in by water.

stop_05_blackfriars_c1.narration: The steamers have changed everything, and within my own memory too. It's a halfpenny or a penny for a short way upriver, twopence if you're going further, and you'll be there before a cab has even cleared the Strand. Half the men you can see going to work on that water used to walk it.
stop_05_blackfriars_c1.scene: The river beside Blackfriars Bridge, 1850: a paddle steamer crowded with passengers pushes through midstream on the right. Below it, worn stone river stairs come down to the water at the bridge's foot. Two or three small wooden wherries with waiting watermen lie moored at the stairs.

points.label: river steamer
points.line: She's carrying more people in a single trip than a wherry could manage in a whole day, and she doesn't much care which way the tide is running. That's the entire story, really, in one boat.

points.label: stone steps
points.line: Those stairs are how you get down from the road to the water, and they're older than the bridge itself. Every set of river stairs has its own watermen who reckon the place belongs to them.

points.label: waiting wherries
points.line: Those are wherries, waiting. A waterman rows a licensed boat and served seven years to learn how, and the steam is quietly taking his living away while he sits there. It's a trade going out in front of us.

stop_05_blackfriars_c2.narration: This is still the old bridge, Mr Mylne's, built of Portland stone and opened in 1769, with nine low arches carrying everything you see. It has stood for eighty years and it's beginning to show every one of them. They say the stone is wearing through and it'll have to come down before long.
stop_05_blackfriars_c2.scene: Old Blackfriars Bridge, London 1850, seen along its length: Portland stone, low elliptical arches, a horse-drawn omnibus taking the centre of the roadway with foot passengers to the sides and no rail between them. One great stone arch is visible below at the right where the bridge meets the water. Riverside chimneys smoke in the distance on the left.

points.label: horse omnibus
points.line: Carriages down the middle and people on foot to the sides, with no rail between them. You learn to walk close to the parapet and not to think about it too much.

points.label: stone arch
points.line: Nine arches, and the water goes through them a good deal faster than it looks. The watermen say that shooting a bridge is the quickest way to drown on purpose, and they're not altogether joking.

points.label: smoking chimneys
points.line: Wharves and works and warehouses, all of them burning coal right at the water's edge, because that's where the coal arrives. The river feeds the smoke, and then the smoke settles back down on the river.

stop_05_blackfriars_c4.narration: Look over the side at the boys down there in the mud. They're not waiting for the boats, they're waiting for the tide. When the water goes out it leaves the whole floor of the river open to anybody bold enough to walk about on it, and there's always somebody bold enough.
stop_05_blackfriars_c4.scene: Looking down from Blackfriars Bridge, 1850, onto the exposed foreshore at low tide: two or three barefoot boys in ragged clothes work the mud below on the left, picking up coal and scraps. On the bridge roadway above to the right, a horse cab passes. Brown water, dark mud, coal smoke overhead.

points.label: mudlark boys
points.line: We call them mudlarks. They're after coal first, then bones and rope and bits of iron, and every piece of it gets sold on to somebody who asks no questions. A middling day comes to about threepence.

points.label: horse cab
points.line: Even up here the cab has to give way to a drove of sheep. London still walks its dinner to market on the hoof, straight over this bridge and into the city.

stop_05_blackfriars.transitionOut: Come down the stairs with me now, and mind how you go. I'd like to finish where everything in this city ends up eventually.

arrival.line: Watch your footing here. This is the foreshore at low water, and it's the bottom of London in every sense you care to name. Everything the town drops or loses or pours away arrives down here twice a day when the tide goes out, and there are people whose whole living is waiting for it to happen.
arrival.scene: The Thames foreshore at low tide near Paul's Wharf, London 1850, standing on the mud. The dome of St Paul's rises pale above the wharf buildings on the skyline. In the middle distance a wooden barge lies grounded on her side in the ooze. On the left, slimy stone wharf steps come down from the quay to the shore, green with weed at the bottom.

points.label: St Paul's dome
points.line: From up on the hill that dome belongs to the bishops and the bankers. From down here in the mud it's the very same dome, and it looks at us just the same way. I've always rather liked that about it.

points.label: Grounded boat
points.line: She was run aground on purpose at high water, so the men could unload her straight onto the shore with no wharf to pay for and no crane to wait on. The flood will lift her off again this evening, none the worse.

points.label: Wharf steps
points.line: Those steps are green with weed up to the waterline, and that mark is where the tide will be again by evening. Don't go below it, and never turn your back on the river.

stop_06_thames_foreshore_c1.narration: Those children are working, not playing. They come down at the ebb and go out over the mud with bare feet, because boots are worth more than anything they're likely to find and can't be spared to the ooze. Glass and nails are what carelessness costs you down here, and there's nothing to be done about a cut but carry on.
stop_06_thames_foreshore_c1.scene: A single photograph of one continuous scene, never split into panels or halves. The Thames foreshore at low water, London 1850, standing down on the mud itself. Three barefoot children in ragged clothes stoop over the exposed mud in the middle of the frame, one holding a small sack. On the left, a flight of worn stone river stairs comes down from the quay wall into the shore, slimy and green at the foot. Beyond the wharf roofs behind them, the dome of St Paul's stands pale against a smoky sky. Wet mud, scattered rope and coal, low grey light.

points.label: stone steps
points.line: Every set of stairs like these has its own little crew of children, and they don't go trespassing on each other. There's rather more law among them down here than you'd suppose.

points.label: mudlark children
points.line: Coal is what they're hoping for, fallen from the barges. A gentleman went about last year writing all this down, asking children like these what they earned. It was printed in the papers, and nothing changed.

stop_06_thames_foreshore_c2.narration: This is the working front of the greatest church in England: stairs and chains and timber piles, and barges nosing in on the tide. The coal that warms the city comes up on this water, and the men who unload it will never once be asked inside the building on the hill above them.
stop_06_thames_foreshore_c2.scene: The working riverside beneath St Paul's, London 1850: the cathedral dome pale above the wharf roofs, a flight of wooden wharf stairs descending to the mud on the left, and heavy iron mooring chains with timber piles on the right where barges are made fast. Low tide, exposed mud, working boats.

points.label: wharf stairs
points.line: Those wharf stairs are slick as glass at the ebb. The river gives you about two hours at the bottom of the tide and then takes them back again, and it doesn't ask whether you've finished.

points.label: chains and piles
points.line: The chains and the timber piles hold the landing to its work while the barges strain against them. Every bit of iron you can see down here is worth money to somebody, which is why so little of it is ever loose.

stop_06_thames_foreshore_c4.narration: A basket like mine will hold whatever sells. Violets in the spring, oranges when the flowers are finished, watercress all the year round, and I've carried all three in this one. That's the whole of my security, and it's the same security as theirs down there. What you can carry, and whether anybody wants it today.
stop_06_thames_foreshore_c4.scene: A flower seller stands on the Thames foreshore at low tide, 1850, her mended wicker basket on her arm in the near left foreground. Behind her a barge sits grounded in the mud to the right, chains slack. The dome of St Paul's rises pale over the wharves in the distance on the right.

points.label: mud barge
points.line: She'll lie there in the ooze until the water comes back for her, and the mud will be turned over twice by the children before that happens. Nothing stays on this shore for very long.

points.label: wicker basket
points.line: Wicker, mended twice, and it will outlast this shawl of mine. A basket is the one real tool of my trade, and I'd sooner lose a whole day's stock than lose it.

stop_06_thames_foreshore.transitionOut: And that's the end of it, down here in the mud where everything the city drops comes to rest. You've seen the top of the hill and the bottom of the river in a single morning, and there isn't much of London that doesn't sit somewhere between the two. My name's Nell Baker, and I'll be at the top of Ludgate Hill tomorrow at five with whatever's fresh. Mind those steps on the way up, they're slippery. And thank you for walking with me.
